questions.q: Why are young people especially vulnerable to peer pressure?

questions.q: How does the desire to fit in affect people's behaviour?

questions.q: Do you think social media has made peer pressure stronger?

questions.q: How can young people be helped to resist negative peer pressure?

questions.q: Some say peer pressure decreases as people get older. Do you agree?

questions.q: Do you think loneliness will become a bigger problem in the future?

questions.q: Some say technology is the main cause of modern loneliness. Do you agree?

questions.q: How do you think we will communicate in the future?

questions.q: How can people avoid becoming too dependent on digital communication?

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of communicating mainly through text?

questions.q: Some say technology is making face-to-face conversation a dying skill. Do you agree?

questions.q: What are the consequences of companies collecting so much personal data?
questions.answer: The consequences are significant and often hidden. Companies use our data to target advertising with [[uncanny]] precision, which can feel manipulative. More seriously, large data collections are vulnerable to breaches, potentially exposing people to fraud and identity theft. There is also the broader concern of this information being used to influence our behaviour and opinions. Essentially, it creates a huge [[imbalance]] of power that can [[undermine]] individual autonomy.

questions.q: How does the loss of privacy affect society?
questions.answer: A society without privacy can become one of pervasive surveillance, which can have a [[chilling effect]] on free expression. If people feel constantly watched, they may [[self-censor]] and conform, which is unhealthy for democracy. The concentration of personal data in a few powerful hands also creates opportunities for manipulation on a mass scale. So the erosion of privacy is not merely a personal issue; it has profound [[implications]] for freedom itself.

questions.q: Do you think privacy will exist in the future?
questions.answer: I am somewhat pessimistic, though not entirely without hope. As technology becomes ever more [[pervasive]], with smart devices and surveillance everywhere, maintaining privacy will become increasingly difficult. However, I am hopeful that growing public awareness and stronger regulations, like data protection laws, could push back against this trend. So while privacy as we once knew it may diminish, I believe the fight to [[preserve]] a meaningful degree of it will [[intensify]].

questions.q: What can be done to better protect people's online privacy?
questions.answer: Solutions must operate at multiple levels. Governments should enforce robust data protection laws that give people genuine control over their information, like Europe's regulations. Companies must be more [[transparent]] about how they use data. On an individual level, education about privacy settings, strong passwords and cautious sharing is vital. questions.q: Are there any benefits to sharing personal data with companies?

So the benefits are real, but they should come from an informed, [[voluntary]] exchange rather than covert [[exploitation]].

questions.q: Some say if you have nothing to hide, privacy does not matter. Do you agree?

We all have private thoughts and information that are simply [[nobody else's business]], regardless of innocence. This argument also dangerously assumes those in power will always act benevolently. In my view, defending privacy is about protecting freedom itself, not [[concealing]] anything [[sinister]].

questions.q: How has the way people get news changed over the years?
questions.answer: The change has been revolutionary. In the past, people relied on scheduled TV bulletins and printed newspapers, receiving curated news once or twice a day. questions.q: Why do you think fake news spreads so easily?
questions.answer: Several factors are at play. Social media algorithms tend to prioritise engaging content, and false or sensational stories are often more [[provocative]] than the truth. People also share things impulsively without verifying them, especially if they confirm existing beliefs. The lack of traditional editorial gatekeepers online means misinformation can spread [[unchecked]]. Combined with a general decline in media literacy, this creates the perfect conditions for falsehoods to [[proliferate]].

questions.q: How does the media influence public opinion?
questions.answer: The media [[wields]] enormous influence over public opinion. By choosing which stories to cover and how to frame them, it shapes what people think is important and how they interpret events. This [[agenda-setting]] power is significant. Repeated exposure to particular viewpoints can gradually shape attitudes, sometimes reinforcing bias. So while a free media is vital for democracy, its power to [[sway]] opinion also carries real responsibility.

questions.q: Do you think traditional newspapers will survive in the future?
questions.answer: In their printed form, I think they will largely decline, as younger generations consume news almost entirely online. However, I do not believe quality journalism itself will disappear; rather, it will continue its shift to digital platforms and subscription models. The [[reputable]] news organisations behind the papers may well [[endure]], just in a different format. So the printed page may fade, but the institution of journalism should [[persist]].

questions.q: What can be done to combat the spread of misinformation?
questions.answer: Tackling this requires a combined effort. Improving media literacy so people can critically [[evaluate]] sources is perhaps the most important long-term solution. Social media platforms must also take greater responsibility, using fact-checking and adjusting algorithms that reward sensationalism. Supporting quality, independent journalism is equally vital. Ultimately, an informed, [[sceptical]] public is the best defence against the [[tide of misinformation]].

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of having 24-hour news?
questions.answer: The advantage is that we are kept constantly informed of breaking events as they unfold, which can be valuable in a crisis. However, the disadvantages are considerable. The pressure to fill airtime often leads to speculation, repetition and [[sensationalism]] over substance. It can also foster a state of perpetual anxiety and [[desensitise]] us to serious events. So constant news offers [[immediacy]] at the cost of depth and perspective.

questions.q: Some say the media focuses too much on negative news. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I largely agree with this. There is a well-known principle in journalism that bad news sells, so outlets tend to prioritise disasters, conflict and scandal, which are more attention-grabbing. This can give people a distorted, overly [[pessimistic]] view of the world, ignoring genuine progress. While reporting problems is important, this relentless [[negativity]] can be [[demoralising]]. A more balanced approach, including constructive news, would be healthier.

questions.q: What impact do video games have on young people?
questions.answer: The impact is genuinely mixed and often exaggerated. On the positive side, many games improve problem-solving, coordination and even teamwork when played socially, and they are a legitimate form of relaxation. However, excessive gaming can lead to addiction, a [[sedentary lifestyle]] and, in some cases, exposure to [[toxic]] online behaviour. So like most things, video games are beneficial [[in moderation]] but harmful to excess.

questions.q: How do you think entertainment will change in the future?
questions.answer: I expect entertainment to become far more [[immersive]] and interactive. Virtual and augmented reality could allow us to step inside stories and games rather than merely watching them. Artificial intelligence may create personalised content tailored precisely to individual tastes. The line between passive viewing and active participation will likely blur. While thrilling, I hope this does not come at the expense of the shared, communal joys that entertainment can [[foster]] and [[preserve]].

questions.q: How can people avoid spending too much time on online entertainment?
questions.answer: Self-discipline and awareness are key. Setting clear time limits and using apps that track usage can prevent hours from [[slipping away]] unnoticed. Consciously scheduling other activities, like exercise, hobbies or socialising, ensures entertainment does not [[crowd out]] everything else. It also helps to remove the [[constant temptation]], perhaps by keeping devices out of reach. Essentially, treating entertainment as a reward rather than a default keeps it in balance.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of on-demand entertainment?
questions.answer: The advantages are obvious: unprecedented convenience, choice and control over what and when we watch. It is tailored to our tastes and available instantly. The disadvantages, however, include the temptation to binge excessively, which can waste time and disrupt sleep. The sheer abundance of choice can also be [[paralysing]], and it can isolate us. So it offers wonderful freedom, but demands [[self-control]] to enjoy without [[overindulging]].

questions.q: Some say people are becoming too passive in how they spend their free time. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I have some sympathy with this view. There is a real tendency to default to passive consumption, like endless scrolling or binge-watching, which requires little effort and can be [[mindless]]. This may come at the expense of more active, [[enriching]] pursuits like exercise, hobbies or socialising. However, I would not generalise too broadly, as many people remain active. It is more a temptation to [[guard against]] than an inevitable decline.

questions.q: At what age do you think children should be allowed to use technology?
questions.answer: This is a difficult question with no perfect answer. I believe very young children should have extremely limited screen time, as their development depends on [[real-world play]] and interaction. As they grow, technology can be gradually introduced, ideally in an educational and supervised way. So rather than a strict age, I favour a [[gradual]], [[age-appropriate]] approach, always emphasising quality of content over quantity of time.

questions.q: How is childhood today different because of technology?
questions.answer: Technology has fundamentally reshaped childhood. Today's children are digital natives, growing up with screens and instant access to information their parents never had. Much of their play, learning and socialising now happens online. While this offers incredible opportunities, it also means less unstructured outdoor play and more [[sedentary]] time. So childhood is arguably more [[stimulating]] but also more [[screen-bound]] than it was a generation ago.

questions.q: What effects can too much screen time have on children?
questions.answer: The potential effects are concerning. Excessive screen time seems to be linked to problems with sleep, attention and physical health due to [[inactivity]]. It may also [[hinder]] the development of social skills and language if it replaces real interaction. There are concerns about exposure to unsuitable content too. So while technology has benefits, an excess can genuinely [[impair]] a child's healthy development, both physically and socially.

questions.q: How can technology be used positively in children's education?
questions.answer: Used well, technology can be a wonderful educational tool. Interactive apps and games can make learning engaging and cater to different learning styles. It gives children access to a vast world of knowledge and can help those with special needs. Educational videos can explain complex ideas vividly. The key is that it should be used [[purposefully]] as a [[supplement]] to good teaching, not as a [[substitute]] for it.

questions.q: Do you think future generations will be even more dependent on technology?
questions.answer: Almost certainly, yes. As technology becomes ever more woven into every aspect of life, future generations will grow up with it as an [[inseparable]] part of their existence. This dependence will likely deepen, which brings both opportunities and risks. My hope is that alongside this, we will develop a stronger culture of digital wellbeing, teaching children to use technology [[intentionally]] and to maintain a healthy balance rather than being [[consumed]] by it.

questions.q: How can parents keep their children safe online?
questions.answer: Parents can take several practical steps. Using [[parental controls]] and age-appropriate settings helps filter unsuitable content. Keeping devices in shared family spaces rather than bedrooms allows for supervision. Most importantly, maintaining open, honest communication so children feel able to report anything [[troubling]] is vital. Educating children about online risks, like strangers and scams, [[empowers]] them. Ultimately, a combination of supervision and education is the best protection.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of children learning to code at a young age?
questions.answer: The advantages are significant. Coding teaches [[logical thinking]], problem-solving and creativity, and it [[equips]] children with a highly valuable skill for the future job market. It can also be genuinely fun and empowering. The potential disadvantages are that it adds to screen time and academic pressure, and it should not [[crowd out]] other essential activities like play and physical exercise. So it is a valuable skill, provided it is kept in balance and not forced.

questions.q: Some say technology is robbing children of a real childhood. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I partly agree, though I think it is a little [[overstated]]. There is a legitimate concern that excessive screen time is replacing the outdoor play, imagination and face-to-face friendships that define a healthy childhood. However, technology also offers genuine benefits and is simply the reality of the modern world. So rather than [[demonising]] it, I believe the answer lies in [[moderation]], ensuring children still enjoy a rich, balanced upbringing.

data.description: The role of tradition in modern life and whether it is being lost.

questions.q: Do you think traditions are still important in modern society?
questions.answer: I believe they are more important than ever. In a rapidly changing, globalised world, traditions provide a vital sense of identity, continuity and belonging. They connect us to our history and to one another. While some outdated customs deserve to fade, I think the core traditions that [[bind]] a community together are worth [[preserving]]. They give life a certain meaning and rhythm that [[modernity]] alone cannot provide.

questions.q: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
questions.answer: To some extent, yes, though it varies. Young people, being more exposed to global culture and modern lifestyles, sometimes view certain traditions as [[outdated]] or irrelevant. However, I would not say they have abandoned tradition entirely; many still take great pride in their [[cultural roots]], just alongside a more modern outlook. So there is a shift in emphasis, but I think the connection to heritage remains, merely [[reinterpreted]] in a contemporary context.

questions.q: Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?
questions.answer: Several forces are at work. Globalisation and the dominance of Western culture have [[homogenised]] lifestyles, making some local customs seem less relevant. Urbanisation and modern, busy lives also leave less time for elaborate traditional practices. Additionally, as older generations pass away, knowledge and skills are sometimes not passed on. So it is really a combination of cultural [[dilution]] and the practical pressures of modern life [[eroding]] them.

questions.q: How do traditions help bring communities together?
questions.answer: Traditions play a powerful unifying role. Shared festivals, rituals and customs create a sense of collective identity and belonging, reminding people that they are part of something larger than themselves. They bring people together to celebrate or mourn collectively, strengthening social bonds. This shared heritage fosters mutual understanding and [[solidarity]]. In essence, traditions act as a kind of [[social glue]] that reinforces community [[cohesion]].

questions.q: Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
questions.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. While some traditions will inevitably fade, I believe the most meaningful ones will [[endure]], perhaps in modified forms. There is actually a growing appreciation for heritage as a counterbalance to globalisation, with many people actively seeking to [[revive]] old customs. Technology can also help document and share them. So rather than vanishing, I think traditions will [[evolve]], adapting to remain relevant in a changing world.

questions.q: What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
questions.answer: A [[concerted effort]] is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. Documenting traditions and supporting the [[artisans]] and elders who hold this knowledge is also vital. Governments and communities can organise festivals and cultural events to keep customs alive and visible. Essentially, making tradition feel relevant and engaging to the young is the key to its [[continuity]].

questions.q: Are there any disadvantages to holding on to old traditions?
questions.answer: Yes, tradition can have a darker side. Some customs are rooted in outdated beliefs and can [[perpetuate]] inequality or harmful practices, such as those that discriminate against certain groups. Blindly following tradition can also [[stifle]] progress and individual freedom. So while I value heritage, I think it is important to be discerning, preserving what enriches us while being willing to [[discard]] customs that are genuinely harmful or unjust.

questions.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. So while the risk of [[homogenisation]] is real, cultures can also prove remarkably [[resilient]] and adaptive.

questions.q: Why do you think festivals are important?
questions.answer: Festivals serve several important purposes. They provide a much-needed break from routine and an occasion for joy and celebration. More deeply, they reinforce cultural identity and bring communities and families together in shared rituals. They also pass traditions from one generation to the next. In my view, this sense of [[collective]] celebration and [[belonging]] is something people fundamentally need, which is why festivals remain so [[cherished]] across cultures.

questions.q: How are festivals celebrated differently now compared to the past?
questions.answer: The essence remains, but the style has changed. In the past, celebrations were often simpler and more community-focused, with everyone participating directly. Today, festivals have become more [[commercialised]], with an emphasis on spending and consumption. Technology has also changed things; people now share their celebrations on social media. So while festivals are still meaningful, some argue they have lost a degree of [[authenticity]], becoming more about [[consumerism]] than genuine tradition.

questions.q: What effect does commercialisation have on traditional festivals?
questions.answer: The effect is [[double-edged]]. On one hand, commercialisation can boost the economy and [[raise a festival's profile]], making it more widely known. On the other, it can [[dilute]] the festival's original spiritual or cultural meaning, reducing it to a shopping opportunity. The genuine sentiment behind the celebration can get lost amid the advertising and pressure to spend. So it brings visibility, but often at the cost of authenticity and true significance.

questions.q: How do festivals contribute to a country's economy?
questions.answer: Festivals can be a significant economic driver. They boost spending on food, gifts, clothing and travel, benefiting countless businesses. Major festivals also attract tourists, generating substantial revenue for the hospitality and transport sectors. They create [[seasonal employment]] too. So beyond their cultural value, festivals are a genuine economic [[stimulus]], injecting money into local economies and showcasing a country's culture to a global audience, which is a real [[asset]].

questions.q: Do you think traditional festivals will remain popular in the future?
questions.answer: I believe they will, though they will continue to evolve. While the way we celebrate may change, the fundamental human need for community, joy and shared meaning will ensure festivals [[endure]]. There may even be a [[resurgence]] of interest as people seek authenticity in an increasingly digital world. So while some may become more modernised or commercial, I think the core appeal of festivals will [[persist]] and remain relevant for generations.

questions.q: How can the true spirit of festivals be preserved?
questions.answer: Preserving the spirit requires conscious effort. Emphasising the values behind the festival, such as togetherness, gratitude or reflection, rather than just the material aspects, is important. Involving young people in traditional practices and explaining their meaning helps too. Communities can prioritise participation over consumption. Essentially, if we consciously focus on the [[essence]] of a festival rather than its [[commercial trappings]], its true spirit can [[thrive]].

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of large public celebrations?
questions.answer: Large public celebrations create a wonderful, [[vibrant]] atmosphere and a powerful sense of collective joy and unity. They boost tourism and local pride. However, the disadvantages include practical issues like [[overcrowding]], noise, litter and strain on public services. There can also be safety concerns. So while they are culturally and economically valuable, they require careful management to minimise the [[disruption]] and ensure everyone can enjoy them safely.

questions.q: Some say festivals have become too commercial. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I largely agree with this observation. Many festivals now seem dominated by advertising, sales and pressure to spend, which can [[overshadow]] their original cultural or spiritual meaning. The focus has shifted, in some cases, from [[togetherness]] to consumerism. That said, this is not universal, and the deeper meaning often survives beneath the commercial surface for those who seek it. So it is a real trend to resist, but not an [[irreversible]] one.

questions.q: How important is food to a country's culture?
questions.answer: Food is absolutely central to culture, in my view. It is far more than mere [[sustenance]]; it reflects a nation's history, geography, values and social customs. Sharing a meal is a universal expression of hospitality and community. Traditional dishes carry deep [[sentimental]] and cultural significance, passed down through generations. So I would say cuisine is one of the most [[tangible]] and beloved expressions of a country's identity.

questions.q: How have people's eating habits changed over the years?
questions.answer: Eating habits have changed considerably. In the past, people mostly ate home-cooked, seasonal and local food, often together as a family. Today, busy lifestyles have led to more processed food, takeaways and eating [[on the go]], often alone. [[Portion sizes]] have grown, and international cuisine is now widely available. While this offers more variety and convenience, I think it has come at some cost to health and the [[communal]] nature of dining.

questions.q: Why do you think fast food has become so popular?
questions.answer: Its popularity comes down to a few key factors. Firstly, it is convenient and quick, which suits our increasingly busy, time-poor lifestyles. Secondly, it is relatively cheap and consistently tasty, engineered to appeal to our [[cravings]]. Aggressive marketing has also made it [[ubiquitous]] and aspirational. Unfortunately, this convenience comes at a cost, as many argue its popularity has contributed to rising rates of [[obesity]] and related health problems.

questions.q: How does the availability of international food affect local cuisine?
questions.answer: It has a mixed effect. On the positive side, it enriches our [[culinary]] options and promotes [[cultural exchange]], allowing people to enjoy dishes from around the world. This is broadening and enjoyable. However, there is a concern that the popularity of international chains could [[overshadow]] and threaten traditional local cuisine. So while it adds welcome diversity, it is important that local food traditions are also valued and preserved alongside it.

questions.q: How do you think the way we eat will change in the future?
questions.answer: I anticipate significant changes driven by health and sustainability concerns. Plant-based diets and [[alternative proteins]], like lab-grown meat, are likely to become far more [[mainstream]] as we address the environmental impact of food. Technology may also personalise nutrition. Hopefully, there will be a renewed appreciation for healthy, [[sustainable]] eating. So our diets may become more conscious and innovative, balancing convenience with health and the planet.

questions.q: What can be done to encourage people to eat more healthily?
questions.answer: A range of measures could help. Education about nutrition from a young age is fundamental, so people can make informed choices. Making healthy food more affordable and accessible, while perhaps [[taxing unhealthy options]], can shift behaviour. Clear [[food labelling]] and restrictions on junk food advertising, especially to children, would also help. Ultimately, creating an environment where the healthy choice is the easy, [[appealing]] choice is the most effective approach.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of eating out often?
questions.answer: Eating out offers convenience, saves time on cooking and cleaning, and provides a pleasant social experience and variety. It can be [[a real treat]]. The disadvantages, however, are that it is expensive and often less healthy, as restaurant food tends to be higher in salt, sugar and fat, with larger portions. Doing it too often can [[strain]] both your finances and your health. So it is best enjoyed in [[moderation]].

questions.q: Some say home-cooked food is always better than restaurant food. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I largely agree, particularly regarding health and value. Home cooking allows you to control the ingredients, ensuring meals are fresher, healthier and cheaper, and it can be a rewarding activity. There is also something uniquely [[comforting]] about a home-cooked meal. However, I would not say it is always better; skilled chefs create [[exquisite]] dishes that are hard to [[replicate]] at home. So home cooking is generally healthier, but restaurants offer expertise and occasion.

questions.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
questions.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

questions.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
questions.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

questions.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
questions.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

questions.q: How does travel affect a person's understanding of the world?
questions.answer: Travel is genuinely one of the best forms of education. By experiencing different cultures firsthand, people develop empathy and challenge their own assumptions and prejudices. It reveals both the vast diversity and the fundamental similarities of humanity. This tends to make people more [[tolerant]], worldly and appreciative of what they have at home. In essence, travel [[broadens the mind]] in a way that no book or documentary can fully [[replicate]].

questions.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
questions.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

questions.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
questions.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of tourism for a country?
questions.answer: The advantages are considerable: tourism generates significant income and employment, funds infrastructure, and promotes cultural exchange and international understanding. It can be a real economic [[lifeline]]. The disadvantages include [[environmental degradation]], overcrowding, the erosion of local culture and over-reliance on a volatile industry. So tourism is a powerful economic tool, but a country must balance the pursuit of revenue against protecting its environment and cultural [[integrity]].

questions.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous [[force for good]], funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome [[hinges on]] responsible [[stewardship]] and planning.

questions.q: Why do you think fashion is important to some people?
questions.answer: For many people, fashion is a genuine form of [[self-expression]], allowing them to communicate their personality, mood and identity without words. It can boost confidence and create a sense of belonging to a particular group. For some, it is also an art form and a source of creativity. While I personally value comfort over trends, I completely understand why fashion [[holds such significance]]; it is a powerful, [[visual language]] of identity.

questions.q: Do you think people care more about fashion now than in the past?
questions.answer: In some ways, yes. The rise of social media has made appearance more visible and, arguably, more important, with influencers constantly showcasing new trends. [[Fast fashion]] has also made trendy clothing cheap and accessible, [[fuelling]] constant consumption. However, past eras had their own strong fashion cultures too. So perhaps it is not that people care more, but that fashion has become more fast-paced, [[disposable]] and publicly displayed than ever before.

questions.q: What effect does the fashion industry have on the environment?
questions.answer: The environmental impact is unfortunately severe, particularly from fast fashion. The industry is a major consumer of water and a significant source of pollution and carbon emissions. The culture of buying cheap, disposable clothing generates enormous [[textile waste]], much of which ends up in landfill. So while fashion brings joy and self-expression, its current [[unsustainable]] model [[exacts a heavy toll]] on the planet that urgently needs addressing.

questions.q: How does fashion influence young people?
questions.answer: Fashion has a [[powerful hold]] on young people. It is closely tied to identity and social acceptance, so what they wear can strongly affect their confidence and sense of belonging. Trends spread rapidly through social media, creating pressure to keep up, which can be expensive and stressful. While fashion can be a positive outlet for creativity, this [[relentless]] pressure to conform can also [[breed insecurity]] and unhealthy comparison.

questions.q: How do you think fashion will change in the future?
questions.answer: I anticipate sustainability will become a [[driving force]]. As awareness of fast fashion's harm grows, I expect a shift towards more durable, ethical and recycled clothing, and a move away from [[throwaway culture]]. Technology may also personalise fashion, and digital or virtual clothing could even emerge. So I am hopeful the future of fashion will be more sustainable, more conscious, and perhaps less [[wasteful]] than the current model.

questions.q: What can be done to make fashion more sustainable?
questions.answer: Several changes are needed. On the industry side, brands should adopt ethical, eco-friendly production and be more transparent. Consumers can play a huge role by buying less, choosing quality over quantity, and embracing [[second-hand]] or recycled clothing. Repairing and reusing garments rather than discarding them also helps. Ultimately, moving away from a throwaway mindset towards more [[durable]], [[considered consumption]] is the most impactful solution.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of following fashion trends?
questions.answer: Following trends can be fun and allows people to feel current, confident and part of a community. It is a [[creative outlet]] and can help people fit in socially. The disadvantages, though, are that constantly chasing trends is expensive, contributes to environmental waste, and can suppress genuine individuality. It can also foster insecurity. So while there is joy in it, an [[obsessive]] pursuit of trends can become both costly and [[superficial]].

questions.q: Some say fashion is a waste of money. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I only partly agree. Excessive spending on constantly changing trends, particularly disposable fast fashion, can certainly be wasteful and financially [[imprudent]]. However, I would not dismiss fashion entirely, as it is a [[legitimate]] form of self-expression and creativity that brings people genuine joy and confidence. Investing in quality, lasting pieces is also sensible. So it is not inherently a waste; it becomes one only when pursued excessively and [[impulsively]].

questions.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
questions.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

questions.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
questions.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

questions.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
questions.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

questions.q: How does having free time affect people's quality of life?
questions.answer: Free time is essential for a good quality of life. It provides the space to rest, [[recharge]] and pursue the activities and relationships that bring us joy and meaning. Without adequate leisure, people risk burnout, stress and a [[diminished]] sense of wellbeing. Free time allows us to be more than just workers. So I would argue that leisure is not a luxury but a fundamental necessity for a healthy, [[rounded]] existence.

questions.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
questions.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

questions.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
questions.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

questions.q: Are there any downsides to spending too much time on hobbies?
questions.answer: There can be, if taken to an extreme. While hobbies are healthy, an obsessive devotion to one could lead to neglecting responsibilities, relationships or work. Some hobbies can also become expensive. If a hobby turns into an escape from dealing with real problems, that is unhealthy too. So like most things, hobbies are wonderful in [[moderation]], but they should [[complement]] a balanced life rather than [[consume]] it entirely.

questions.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

data.description: How and why people buy, and the culture of consumption.

questions.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
questions.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

questions.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
questions.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

questions.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
questions.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

questions.q: What impact does consumerism have on society?
questions.answer: Consumerism has a profound and mixed impact. It drives economic growth and provides jobs, which is beneficial. However, it also fuels [[materialism]], encouraging people to equate happiness with possessions, which many would argue is [[illusory]]. It contributes significantly to environmental degradation through waste and [[resource depletion]]. It can also foster debt and dissatisfaction. So while it powers the economy, unchecked consumerism carries serious social and environmental costs.

questions.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
questions.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

questions.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
questions.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of online shopping?
questions.answer: The advantages are clear: convenience, a vast selection, easy price comparison and often lower prices, all from home. It is a great [[time-saver]]. The disadvantages include the inability to physically examine products before buying, delivery delays, the environmental cost of packaging and transport, and the temptation to [[overspend]]. It also lacks the social experience of physical shopping. So it offers wonderful convenience, but with some real [[trade-offs]] in experience and impact.

questions.q: Some say buying things makes people happy. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I only partly agree. There is undeniably a short-term thrill in acquiring something new, so buying can bring a [[fleeting]] sense of pleasure. However, many people feel this happiness is temporary and superficial, quickly fading in a cycle sometimes called the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Lasting happiness tends to come from experiences and relationships, not possessions. So while shopping offers momentary joy, relying on it for happiness is ultimately [[hollow]] and unfulfilling.

data.description: How cultures influence one another in an interconnected world.

questions.q: Do you think cultural globalisation is a positive development?
questions.answer: I see it as a genuinely [[double-edged]] phenomenon. On the positive side, it fosters greater understanding, tolerance and exchange between cultures, and lets us enjoy the best of what the world offers, from food to film. However, there is a real risk that it leads to cultural [[homogenisation]], where dominant cultures [[overwhelm]] local ones. So while I appreciate the connection it brings, I believe we must actively work to preserve cultural diversity alongside it.

questions.q: How has globalisation changed local cultures?
questions.answer: The changes are significant. Local cultures have been enriched by exposure to global ideas, technologies and cuisines. However, they have also been challenged, as global brands, media and the English language spread, sometimes [[eclipsing]] local traditions and languages. The result is often a hybrid culture, blending the local and the global. So globalisation has made cultures more [[interconnected]] and diverse in some ways, yet more [[uniform]] in others.

questions.q: What effect does the spread of English have on other languages?
questions.answer: The spread of English as a global [[lingua franca]] has clear benefits, facilitating international communication, business and science. However, it also poses a threat to [[linguistic diversity]]. As English dominates, some smaller languages are being [[marginalised]] and, in extreme cases, are dying out, taking unique cultural knowledge with them. So while a common language is enormously useful, its dominance risks a loss of the rich linguistic heritage that makes humanity so diverse.

questions.q: How does exposure to other cultures affect people?
questions.answer: Exposure to other cultures is generally very positive for people. It tends to make individuals more open-minded, tolerant and [[empathetic]], as they realise there are many valid ways of living. It challenges stereotypes and prejudices. It can also be creatively inspiring, blending ideas in new ways. So while it can occasionally cause a sense of confusion about one's own identity, overall I believe cultural exposure [[broadens horizons]] and [[enriches]] people enormously.

questions.q: Do you think all cultures will eventually become the same?
questions.answer: I do not think so, though they will certainly grow more similar in some respects. While globalisation is a powerful homogenising force, human beings have a deep-seated need for distinct identity and belonging, which tends to make cultures [[resilient]]. We are also seeing movements to actively preserve and revive local traditions. So rather than becoming identical, I expect cultures to blend and influence one another while retaining their [[distinctive]] [[essence]].

questions.q: How can countries protect their cultural identity in a globalised world?
questions.answer: There are several strategies. Governments can support and fund local arts, languages, film and traditions to ensure they thrive. Education that [[instils]] pride in one's heritage is fundamental. Protecting local media and industries from being entirely overwhelmed by [[global giants]] also helps. Crucially, this should be done not by rejecting outside influence, but by celebrating and promoting one's own culture so that it remains [[vibrant]] and valued.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of a globalised world?
questions.answer: The advantages are substantial: greater economic opportunity, the [[free flow of ideas]] and technology, cultural exchange, and international cooperation on shared problems. It has lifted many out of poverty. The disadvantages include cultural homogenisation, growing inequality, the exploitation of cheaper labour, and increased vulnerability to global crises, as the pandemic showed. So globalisation is a powerful force for connection and progress, but one with significant [[inequalities]] and [[vulnerabilities]].

questions.q: Some say globalisation mainly benefits wealthy countries. Do you agree?
questions.answer: There is considerable truth to this, though it is not the whole picture. It is often argued that wealthy nations and large corporations reap the greatest rewards, while poorer countries may suffer exploitation and cultural erosion. The benefits are undeniably [[unevenly]] distributed. However, globalisation has arguably also lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty in developing nations. So while the [[playing field]] is far from level, I would not say the benefits are exclusively for the [[privileged]].

data.description: The role of music and creative arts in society and individual life.

questions.q: Why do you think music is important to people?
questions.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

questions.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
questions.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

questions.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
questions.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

questions.q: How important are the arts to society?
questions.answer: I believe the arts are absolutely vital, though often [[undervalued]]. They enrich our lives, [[provoke thought]], and allow us to explore and express the full range of human experience. The arts preserve culture and history, foster empathy by exposing us to different perspectives, and can even drive social change. Economically, the creative industries are significant too. So far from being a luxury, the arts are, in my view, essential to a civilised and [[reflective]] society.

questions.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
questions.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

questions.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
questions.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

questions.q: Are there advantages to studying an arts subject rather than a science?
questions.answer: Certainly. Arts subjects develop invaluable skills like critical thinking, creativity, communication and empathy, which are highly transferable and increasingly prized by employers. They encourage us to [[grapple with]] complex human questions. The perceived disadvantage is that arts degrees are sometimes seen as less directly employable than sciences. However, I think this is often overstated, as the skills they cultivate are genuinely [[versatile]]. So both paths have distinct and equal [[merit]].

questions.q: Some say art is not as important as science. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I firmly disagree with ranking them this way, as they serve different but equally vital purposes. Science advances our material understanding and improves our lives technologically, which is crucial. But art nourishes our emotional and spiritual lives, fosters empathy, and gives meaning to human existence. A world with science but no art would be efficient yet [[soulless]]. So rather than one being more important, I see them as [[complementary]] pillars of a [[flourishing]] civilisation.

data.description: Individual and collective responsibility for protecting the environment.

questions.q: Whose responsibility is it to protect the environment?
questions.answer: I believe it is a shared responsibility, though the [[burden falls unevenly]]. Individuals certainly have a role through their daily choices, but honestly, their impact is limited compared to that of governments and large corporations. Governments must implement effective policy and regulation, while industries must change their practices. So while everyone should do their part, I think the greatest responsibility lies with those who hold the power to [[enact]] [[systemic change]].

questions.q: Are individuals or governments more effective at protecting the environment?
questions.answer: While individual actions are valuable and add up, I would argue governments are far more effective due to their [[scale of influence]]. A single person recycling makes a small difference, but a government can regulate entire industries, invest in renewable energy and shape behaviour through law. That said, individual pressure and voting ultimately influence what governments do. So the two are [[interconnected]], but the [[leverage]] of government is undeniably greater.

questions.q: Why do you think some people do not care about the environment?
questions.answer: There are several reasons. For some, environmental problems feel distant and abstract, so they do not feel a sense of urgency. Others prioritise immediate economic concerns, like putting food on the table, over long-term issues. There is also a feeling of [[helplessness]], that individual action is [[futile]]. Additionally, some are simply unaware or misinformed. So it is usually a mix of [[apathy]], immediate priorities and a sense of powerlessness.

questions.q: How does environmental damage affect people's lives?
questions.answer: The effects are increasingly tangible and severe. Pollution directly harms public health, causing respiratory and other illnesses. Climate change brings extreme weather, threatening homes, food security and [[livelihoods]], especially for the poor. The degradation of natural resources also affects economies and can even fuel conflict over scarce resources. So environmental damage is not an abstract issue; it has profound and growing [[repercussions]] for human health, [[prosperity]] and stability.

questions.q: Are you optimistic about the future of the environment?
questions.answer: I am cautiously optimistic, though the challenges are [[daunting]]. On one hand, the scale of problems like climate change is alarming, and progress often feels too slow. On the other hand, awareness has never been higher, technology in renewable energy is advancing rapidly, and younger generations are deeply committed to the cause. So while I have real concerns, I believe human [[ingenuity]] and growing collective will give us genuine [[grounds for hope]].

questions.q: What can ordinary people do to help the environment?
questions.answer: There is a surprising amount individuals can do. Reducing consumption and waste, recycling, and being [[mindful]] of energy and water use all help. Choosing sustainable transport, like walking or public transit, and eating less meat can significantly cut one's [[carbon footprint]]. Beyond personal habits, supporting green businesses and, crucially, voting for environmentally responsible policies [[amplifies]] our impact. Collectively, these individual choices can drive genuine change.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of strict environmental laws?
questions.answer: The advantages are clear: strict laws can effectively [[curb]] pollution, protect natural resources and drive innovation in clean technology, safeguarding public health and the planet. The potential disadvantages are economic; such regulations can increase costs for businesses and consumers and may, in the short term, affect certain industries and jobs. However, I believe the long-term benefits far [[outweigh]] these costs, though a balanced, [[well-planned transition]] is essential.

questions.q: Some say economic growth is more important than protecting the environment. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I strongly disagree with framing them as opposites. This is a [[short-sighted]] view, because a healthy environment is actually the foundation of long-term economic prosperity; you cannot have a thriving economy on a ruined planet. Furthermore, the green economy itself is a huge source of growth and jobs. So rather than a trade-off, I believe sustainable development, where growth and protection go hand in hand, is not only possible but [[imperative]] and [[mutually reinforcing]].

data.description: Global warming, its causes, and the response to it.

questions.q: How serious a problem do you think climate change is?
questions.answer: I consider it one of the most serious challenges facing humanity, if not the most serious. The scientific consensus is overwhelming, and we are already witnessing its effects through more frequent extreme weather, rising sea levels and disrupted ecosystems. Its potential to cause widespread displacement, food insecurity and conflict is genuinely alarming. So while some still [[downplay]] it, I believe it is an [[existential]] threat that demands urgent, [[decisive]] action.

questions.q: Do you think richer or poorer countries should do more to fight climate change?
questions.answer: This is a matter of both responsibility and capability. I believe richer, industrialised nations bear a greater responsibility, as they have contributed the most historical emissions and have the financial resources to lead. It seems only fair for them to do more, including helping poorer nations. However, developing countries, some of which are now major emitters, must also participate. So the burden should be shared [[equitably]], with the wealthy [[shouldering]] a [[proportionate]] load.

questions.q: What are the main effects of climate change on people?
questions.answer: The effects on people are wide-ranging and increasingly severe. More intense heatwaves, floods and storms directly threaten lives and homes. Changing weather patterns disrupt agriculture, [[jeopardising]] food security and livelihoods. Rising seas endanger coastal communities, potentially creating large numbers of [[climate refugees]]. There are also serious health impacts. So climate change is not merely an environmental issue; it is a profound [[humanitarian]] one that threatens the stability of entire societies.

questions.q: Why is it difficult for countries to agree on climate action?
questions.answer: The difficulty lies in competing national interests. Countries worry that ambitious climate action will harm their own economies and competitiveness, so many are reluctant to act unless others do too. There are also disputes over who is most responsible and who should bear the costs. Powerful industries [[lobby against]] change as well. So despite the shared threat, short-term [[self-interest]] and a lack of trust often [[hinder]] the global cooperation required.

questions.q: Do you think we can still prevent the worst effects of climate change?
questions.answer: I believe we still can, but the window is closing rapidly and it will require unprecedented effort. The technology and knowledge to transition to a clean economy largely exist; what is often lacking is the [[political will]] and global cooperation. If we act decisively now, we can still limit the damage, though some impacts are already [[inevitable]]. So I remain hopeful, but only if we treat it with the urgency it truly [[warrants]].

questions.q: What are the most effective ways to tackle climate change?
questions.answer: The most effective solutions involve rapidly [[transitioning away from]] fossil fuels towards renewable energy like solar and wind. Improving energy efficiency and protecting and restoring forests, which absorb carbon, are also crucial. Government policy is key, from [[carbon pricing]] to investment in green technology. Individual lifestyle changes help too. Essentially, it requires a coordinated [[overhaul]] of our energy, transport and consumption systems on a global scale.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of switching to renewable energy?
questions.answer: The advantages are compelling: renewables are clean, produce no carbon emissions, and are increasingly cheap and inexhaustible, enhancing energy security. They also create new jobs. The disadvantages include the high initial cost of infrastructure, and the fact that sources like solar and wind are [[intermittent]], requiring storage solutions. Transitioning also affects existing fossil fuel industries. So while there are real [[hurdles]], the long-term benefits make it a clearly [[worthwhile]] shift.

questions.q: Some say individuals can do little about climate change. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I partly agree but find the statement [[disempowering]]. It is true that systemic change by governments and industry is far more impactful than individual action alone, so no one should feel the entire burden rests on them. However, I disagree that individuals are powerless. Collectively, our consumer choices, our voices and, above all, our votes exert real pressure that drives the bigger changes. So individual action is not [[futile]]; it is part of a larger [[momentum]].

questions.q: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?
questions.answer: It really depends on one's priorities and stage of life. Cities offer better job opportunities, [[amenities]], healthcare and a vibrant social life, which many find appealing. The countryside, by contrast, offers peace, clean air, space and a stronger sense of community. Personally, I appreciate the convenience of the city for now, but I can see the [[profound appeal]] of a quieter rural life later. So neither is objectively better; each suits different needs and [[temperaments]].

questions.q: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
questions.answer: Cities have transformed dramatically. They have grown enormously in size and population due to rapid urbanisation, becoming denser and often more [[congested]]. Skylines have risen with skyscrapers, and technology has made them smarter. However, this growth has often [[outpaced]] infrastructure, worsening problems like traffic, pollution and housing shortages. So while cities have become more developed and connected, this expansion has brought significant [[growing pains]].

questions.q: Why do so many people move to cities?
questions.answer: The primary driver is economic opportunity. Cities are hubs of employment, offering far more and better-paid jobs than rural areas, which is the biggest [[pull factor]]. They also provide superior access to education, healthcare and services. For many, the appeal of a more exciting, diverse lifestyle is also a draw. So this migration is largely driven by the search for a better standard of living, though it can place enormous [[strain]] on urban [[infrastructure]] and resources.

questions.q: What are the main problems facing large cities today?
questions.answer: Large cities [[grapple with]] numerous interconnected challenges. Traffic congestion and air pollution are among the most visible, harming both quality of life and health. A shortage of affordable housing is another major issue, pushing up costs and inequality. Overcrowded public services, waste management and, in some cases, rising crime add to the burden. So while cities are [[engines of prosperity]], managing this rapid growth sustainably is a [[formidable]] challenge.

questions.q: What do you think cities will be like in the future?
questions.answer: I envision cities becoming smarter and, hopefully, greener. Technology will likely manage traffic, energy and services more efficiently through data. There is a strong push towards more sustainable, [[walkable]] cities with more green spaces and cleaner transport. However, they may also become even more crowded. So I am hopeful the cities of the future will be more [[liveable]] and sustainable, provided planning [[prioritises]] people and the environment over pure expansion.

questions.q: How can cities be made better places to live?
questions.answer: Thoughtful [[urban planning]] is the key. Investing in efficient, affordable public transport reduces congestion and pollution. Creating more green spaces and [[pedestrian areas]] improves wellbeing. Ensuring an adequate supply of affordable housing tackles inequality. Designing [[mixed-use]], walkable neighbourhoods fosters community. Essentially, cities become better when they are planned around the needs of people and the environment, rather than simply cars and commerce.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of urbanisation?
questions.answer: Urbanisation drives economic growth and innovation, and provides better access to jobs, services and opportunities, lifting many out of poverty. Cities are also cultural and intellectual [[hubs]]. However, the disadvantages include [[overcrowding]], pollution, pressure on housing and infrastructure, and the loss of green space and community ties. It can also [[deepen inequality]]. So urbanisation is a powerful engine of progress, but one that must be managed to avoid serious social and environmental costs.

questions.q: Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I do not think halting growth is realistic or desirable, but managing it is essential. Trying to stop urban growth [[outright]] would be difficult and could stifle economic opportunity. However, I strongly agree that governments should guide this growth intelligently, perhaps by developing smaller [[satellite cities]] and improving rural areas to [[ease the pressure]]. So rather than restricting cities, the focus should be on making growth sustainable and balanced.

questions.q: Do you think public transport should be free?
questions.answer: I find the idea appealing, though it is complex. Making public transport free could reduce traffic, cut pollution and help [[lower-income]] people enormously, which are [[compelling]] social benefits. However, it would be extremely expensive to fund and might lead to overcrowding or reduced service quality without careful management. So while I support [[heavily subsidising]] it to keep it affordable, whether it should be entirely free depends on a country's priorities and budget.

questions.q: Is it better to travel by public transport or private car?
questions.answer: Each has its merits, but from a societal viewpoint, public transport is clearly [[preferable]]. It is far more environmentally friendly, reduces congestion, and is cheaper for the user. Private cars, however, offer [[unmatched]] convenience, comfort and flexibility, especially where public transport is poor. So while I personally value the freedom of a car, I believe well-developed public transport is the more sustainable and [[equitable]] option for society as a whole.

questions.q: What are the effects of traffic congestion on cities?
questions.answer: Traffic congestion has serious and costly effects. It wastes an enormous amount of people's time, reducing productivity and quality of life. It significantly worsens air pollution, harming public health and the environment. It also causes frustration and stress for commuters and can [[hamper]] emergency services. Economically, the lost hours and fuel represent a huge [[drain]]. So congestion is far more than an inconvenience; it [[undermines]] a city's efficiency and wellbeing.

questions.q: How does good transport benefit a society?
questions.answer: An efficient transport system is the [[backbone]] of a thriving society. It connects people to jobs, education and services, enhancing opportunity and social mobility. It enables the smooth flow of goods, boosting the economy. Good public transport, in particular, reduces pollution and congestion while providing affordable mobility for all, including those without cars. So investing in transport is not just about convenience; it is fundamental to economic [[prosperity]] and social [[inclusion]].

questions.q: How do you think transport will change in the future?
questions.answer: I anticipate significant transformation. Electric vehicles will likely become the norm, drastically cutting emissions, and [[autonomous]], self-driving cars may reshape how we travel. Cities will probably invest more in cycling, walking and clean public transport. Concepts like [[shared mobility]] could reduce car ownership. So the future of transport is likely to be cleaner, smarter and more [[integrated]], hopefully making our cities less polluted and more liveable.

questions.q: How can traffic problems in cities be solved?
questions.answer: A combination of measures is most effective. Investing heavily in reliable, affordable public transport gives people a genuine alternative to driving. Encouraging cycling and walking through better [[infrastructure]] helps too. Some cities use [[congestion charging]] to [[discourage]] car use in busy areas. Better urban planning that reduces the need to travel far is also valuable. Essentially, the solution lies in making sustainable options more attractive than driving, rather than simply widening roads.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of owning a car?
questions.answer: Owning a car offers tremendous freedom, convenience and comfort, allowing you to travel [[on your own schedule]], which is especially valuable where public transport is limited. The disadvantages, however, are significant: the high costs of purchase, fuel, insurance and maintenance, plus the stress of traffic and parking. There is also the considerable environmental impact. So a car provides genuine [[autonomy]], but at a substantial financial and [[ecological]] cost.

questions.q: Some say cars should be banned from city centres. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I broadly agree with this, at least for private cars in the busiest central areas. Many cities that have [[pedestrianised]] their centres seem to have seen reduced pollution, safer streets and more vibrant public life, which is very appealing. However, it must be done carefully, ensuring excellent public transport alternatives and access for deliveries and those with disabilities. So rather than a [[blanket ban]], I support significantly restricting cars to create more [[liveable]], people-friendly centres.

questions.q: How serious is the problem of pollution in your country?

Air quality often reaches [[hazardous]] levels due to traffic, industry and construction, which [[poses a real threat]] to public health. Water pollution from industrial and domestic waste is also a significant concern. So while there is growing awareness, I would say pollution remains one of our most [[pressing]] environmental and public-health challenges.

questions.q: Which do you think is worse, air pollution or water pollution?
questions.answer: Both are extremely damaging, and it is hard to rank them. Air pollution is perhaps more immediate and [[inescapable]], as we breathe constantly, and it causes widespread respiratory illness. Water pollution, however, is arguably more [[insidious]], contaminating our drinking water and food chain and devastating [[aquatic ecosystems]]. So rather than one being definitively worse, I would say they are both severe problems with different but equally devastating consequences.

questions.q: What are the main causes of pollution in cities?
questions.answer: Urban pollution stems from several sources. Vehicle emissions are a [[primary culprit]], given the sheer density of traffic. Industrial activity and factories release pollutants into the air and water. Construction generates dust, and the burning of fossil fuels for energy contributes heavily. Poor waste management adds to the problem. So it is largely a [[by-product]] of dense population, industry and [[reliance on fossil fuels]] concentrated in a small area.

questions.q: How does pollution affect people's health?
questions.answer: The health impacts of pollution are profound and well-documented. Air pollution causes and worsens respiratory conditions like asthma, as well as heart disease and even cancer, reportedly contributing to millions of [[premature deaths]] globally. Water pollution can cause serious diseases through contaminated drinking water. Vulnerable groups, like children and the elderly, are especially at risk. So pollution is a genuine [[silent killer]], imposing an enormous [[burden]] on public health.

questions.q: Do you think pollution will get better or worse in the future?
questions.answer: I am cautiously hopeful it will improve, though it depends on our actions. On one hand, rapid [[industrialisation]] in developing nations could worsen it in the short term. On the other, growing awareness, stricter regulations, and cleaner technologies like electric vehicles and renewable energy offer real solutions. Many developed cities have already reduced pollution significantly. So with sufficient [[political will]] and innovation, I believe we can [[reverse the trend]], but it is not guaranteed.

questions.q: What can be done to reduce pollution?
questions.answer: Tackling pollution requires action [[on multiple fronts]]. Transitioning to renewable energy and electric transport would [[drastically]] cut emissions. [[Enforcing]] strict regulations on industrial waste and improving public transport are vital. Better waste management and recycling reduce landfill and litter. On an individual level, reducing consumption and waste helps. Ultimately, a combination of regulation, clean technology and changed behaviour offers the most effective path forward.

questions.q: Some solutions to pollution are expensive. Are they worth the cost?
questions.answer: I firmly believe they are worth it, viewed correctly. While measures like transitioning to clean energy carry a high upfront cost, this must be weighed against the enormous, often hidden, costs of pollution itself, from healthcare bills to environmental damage and lost productivity. In truth, the cost of [[inaction]] is far greater. So although the investment is substantial, it is far more [[prudent]] than allowing pollution to [[escalate]] unchecked.

questions.q: Some say factories should be moved away from residential areas. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I largely agree with this as a sensible measure. Locating polluting factories away from where people live can significantly reduce residents' [[direct exposure]] to harmful air and water pollution, protecting public health. However, it is not a complete solution, as pollution still spreads, and it may simply [[shift the burden]] to another community. So while separating industry from homes is beneficial, it must be combined with actually reducing the pollution [[at its source]].
